content: Efforts at the global, regional, national, subnational, and facility levels have been directed toward promoting equitable vaccine access while minimizing wastage. Governments have adopted several strategies during past pandemics, including: 1. Accelerating the regulatory approval process, particularly for vaccine manufacturers’ indemnification requirements. 2. Issuing National Emergency Use Authorizations. 3. Selecting vaccines compatible with the country’s cold chain capacity. 4. Authorizing vaccines based on the World Health Organization’s Emergency Use Listing (EUL), especially in countries lacking mature regulatory structures for rapid vaccine approval. 5. Facilitating expedited customs clearance for vaccines upon arrival. Vaccine delivery strategies should be flexible and adaptable, ensuring the quality of services while using emerging evidence to adjust strategies to enhance vaccination coverage. These strategies must include provisions for hard-to-reach populations, such as refugees, internally displaced persons, individuals in correctional facilities, military camps, homes for the elderly, and those with mobility challenges. Plans should also account for potential disruptions caused by pandemic-related travel restrictions. Engaging private facilities can increase the availability of vaccination sites, while operational outreach and mobile vaccination sites are critical for delivering second doses in remote areas. Ongoing public health programs, such as polio vaccination campaigns or Severe Acute Respiratory Infection (SARI) identification drives, can be leveraged to identify and mobilize key populations for vaccination. Integrated IT platforms should be utilized for registration, tracking, and issuing vaccination certificates, as well as monitoring cold chain status and vaccine availability. A combination of delivery strategies, such as drones for remote areas, mobile vans for sparsely populated regions, and newly established vaccination sites in high-risk locations (e.g., prisons, military zones, mining sites), can help achieve equity-driven goals. Single-dose vaccines should be prioritized for mobile and hard-to-reach populations to minimize logistical challenges. Optimization of supply chain operations has been supported by timely preparation and dissemination of guidelines for operational, supply chain, and waste management planning. Periodic nationwide assessments of cold chain storage capacities are necessary to identify additional equipment needs. Potential funding sources should be identified for acquiring ultra-cold chain equipment, refrigerated trucks, and consumables like fuel for vaccine deliveries. Real-time monitoring of vaccine stocks, enabled by logistics management information systems, allows for need-based redistribution of supplies and reduces vaccine wastage. Best practices for managing vaccines with short expiry dates include establishing governing bodies to monitor expiry and recall batches, conducting rapid vaccination campaigns, and redistributing excess doses based on stock levels and demand. Vaccinating subsequent priority groups can also minimize wastage when uptake among the main priority groups is insufficient. A well-trained and supported workforce is critical for successful vaccination campaigns. Training plans should address the needs of all staff and volunteers involved in vaccination activities, including healthcare workers, community mobilization teams, logistics managers, and vaccine safety monitors. Training can be delivered through various modalities, such as face-to-face sessions, on-the-job training, or virtual environments. Mass training and training-of-trainers programs should be conducted before national vaccination campaigns to prepare staff at all levels. Leveraging professionals from the private sector and non-governmental organizations can supplement workforce capacity. Training platforms should allow for rapid training, even in areas with poor internet connectivity. Supportive supervision of frontline health workers and simulation exercises can help maintain and test capabilities. Enhancing digital literacy in the community and providing incentives, such as food boxes or psychological support for staff, can address stress and fatigue while reducing programmatic errors. Sustaining vaccine acceptance and demand requires a robust communication and community engagement plan. Regular communication through press briefings and scientific discussions with academics, media professionals, and social media influencers can promote transparency and timely dissemination of accurate information. Regular meetings at national, regional, and district levels facilitate information sharing among stakeholders. Multisectoral and public-private partnerships can enhance vaccination roll-out and campaign communications. Political ownership at the highest level, with public vaccinations of leaders and regular statements, can build public trust. Efforts should also focus on addressing vaccine hesitancy among healthcare workers, who are often a priority target group during pandemics. Engaging religious, community, and opinion leaders, including medical professionals, can advocate for vaccination. Proactive social listening and management of misinformation are essential, requiring specialized national capacities for infodemic management. Hotlines and surveys can help understand community perceptions and concerns, while dashboards can provide real-time public information. Media platforms, including television, radio, social media, and print, should be used to disseminate information effectively. Vaccine safety monitoring and management of Adverse Events Following Immunization (AEFI) can be advanced by establishing multidisciplinary teams at the national level and AEFI focal points at subnational levels. Standard operating procedures and digital tools should be used for AEFI reporting and response. Active surveillance systems, preferably electronic, should enable real-time monitoring of adverse events of special interest. Training and retaining healthcare workers, sensitizing vaccine recipients to report AEFI, and deploying medical experts for on-site management of serious AEFI are critical. Free treatment for individuals experiencing serious adverse events should be provided at designated health facilities, with insurance schemes adapted to cover medical care for such cases. Official government websites should be updated rapidly with vaccine safety information, and funding should be allocated for AEFI kits and reporting forms. Proficient data management can be achieved by leveraging immunization monitoring systems. QR codes can verify vaccination status, and holograms on vaccination cards can serve as authentication mechanisms. Dedicated electronic vaccination registries and IT platforms, such as DHIS-2 and Google Spreadsheets, can facilitate real-time planning, analysis, and monitoring of vaccine roll-out. Social media and smartphone chat groups can coordinate and communicate coverage data. Backup systems, such as paper-based registers and tally sheets, should be available for sites without electronic access. Supportive supervision for digital systems and regular feedback on reporting gaps are essential. Costing and financing of pandemic vaccine deployment benefit from mechanisms to monitor fund utilization. Resource mobilization strategies should include domestic resources, grants, loans from international agencies, and support from development partners. Conducting National Deployment and Vaccination Plan (NDVP) costing exercises during inter-pandemic periods can help anticipate needs for different pandemic scenarios.
